title: I/O models
scopeHtml: Scope: blocking, non-blocking, select/poll/epoll, event loops (Nginx, Redis), zero-copy, io_uring and debugging.

notes.title: The I/O problem: waiting is the cost
notes.html:
Most server programs spend nearly all their time waiting for I/O (network, disk), not computing. A CPU does a billion simple steps per second; a network round trip inside a data centre takes about 0.5 ms, which is 500,000 CPU cycles of idleness. The question of "I/O models" is: what does the thread do while it waits?

Numbers worth remembering:

Operation Typical time
L1 cache hit 1 ns
RAM access 100 ns
Syscall (cheap) 100 to 500 ns
Context switch 2 to 5 microseconds
NVMe SSD read 20 to 100 microseconds
Same-datacentre round trip 500 microseconds
HDD seek 5 to 10 ms
Cross-continent round trip 80 to 150 ms

Five classic models (Stevens' UNIX Network Programming):

  1. Blocking I/O
  2. Non-blocking I/O (polling)
  3. I/O multiplexing (select, poll, epoll)
  4. Signal-driven I/O (rare)
  5. Asynchronous I/O (io_uring, Windows IOCP)

Worked example. A server must handle 10,000 connected clients, each sending a small request every 10 s, so about 1,000 requests/s. Each takes 50 microseconds of CPU (5% of one core). The CPU work is tiny; the challenge is managing 10,000 mostly idle sockets. That is the C10K problem (Dan Kegel, 1999). The thread-per-connection answer needs 10,000 threads; the multiplexing answer needs one.

Industry examples. Apache's classic prefork model used one process per connection and hit C10K; Nginx (2004) was written specifically to solve it with an event loop; Node.js, Redis, Netty, Envoy, HAProxy and Go's netpoller all follow the event-driven approach.

Everyday analogy. A waiter who stands at one table until the guests finish their meal (blocking) versus a waiter who moves among many tables and serves whoever is ready (event loop).

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up non-blocking with asynchronous. Non-blocking: the call returns immediately with "not ready". Asynchronous: you submit the operation and are told when it is complete.
  • Quoting C10K without saying what changed (event APIs plus cheap per-connection memory).

notes.title: Blocking I/O and thread-per-connection
notes.html:
With blocking I/O, read() puts the calling thread to sleep until data arrives. Simple code, one thread per connection:

ServerSocket ss = new ServerSocket(8080);
while (true) {
    Socket s = ss.accept();                  // blocks
    new Thread(() -> {
        try (var in = s.getInputStream()) {
            byte[] buf = new byte[4096];
            int n = in.read(buf);            // blocks until bytes arrive
            ...
        }
    }).start();
}

When the thread sleeps the CPU runs someone else, so it is not wasteful of CPU; it is wasteful of memory and scheduler work. Each Linux thread reserves a stack (Java default 1 MB virtual, 8 MB for main thread in C) plus kernel structures (~10 KB). 10,000 threads means about 10 GB of virtual address space, 100+ MB real, and the scheduler deals with thousands of runnable entities, so context switches climb.

Worked example. Tomcat default maximum 200 worker threads (Spring Boot server.tomcat.threads.max=200). If each request calls a database taking 100 ms, throughput caps at 200 / 0.1 = 2,000 requests/s regardless of CPU. If the DB slows to 1 s, the cap drops to 200 requests/s and the rest queue (default accept queue 100): the thread pool is the bottleneck. Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency.

Modern revival. Java 21 virtual threads and Go goroutines make thread-per-request cheap again: the runtime parks the lightweight thread on a blocking call and uses an event loop (epoll) underneath. You write blocking-style code with event-loop scalability. Goroutines start at about 2 to 8 KB of stack; a million is feasible.

Decision gravity. Thread-per-connection is the simplest to write and debug (stack traces make sense); the right default below a few thousand concurrent connections. Moving to an event loop is a rewrite of the I/O layer (one-way-ish); virtual threads let you keep the simple model.

Everyday analogy. Hiring one waiter per table. Easy to manage, but a restaurant with 10,000 tables cannot afford it.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking blocking threads burn CPU. They sleep; the cost is memory, stacks and scheduling.
  • Sizing the pool by CPU cores for I/O-bound work. Pool size for blocking work is about cores x (1 + wait/compute).

notes.title: Non-blocking I/O
notes.html:
A non-blocking socket (O_NONBLOCK) makes read() return immediately with the error EAGAIN (or EWOULDBLOCK) if no data is ready. The thread can then do something else. By itself that leads to busy-polling: loop over all sockets asking "ready yet?", burning CPU.

int flags = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);
ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
if (n < 0 && errno == EAGAIN) { /* nothing yet, do other work */ }

Polling 10,000 sockets with 10,000 read calls takes 10,000 syscalls x ~300 ns = 3 ms per sweep, nearly all returning EAGAIN. Useless without a way to ask the kernel "which of these are ready?". That is I/O multiplexing.

Non-blocking also matters for connect (returns EINPROGRESS, completion signalled as writable) and accept. Note: regular disk files are always "ready", so O_NONBLOCK does nothing for them; epoll cannot wait on disk files. This is why Node.js uses a thread pool (libuv) for file I/O, and why io_uring matters.

Everyday analogy. Checking the oven door every second instead of setting a timer.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing O_NONBLOCK works for regular files.
  • Forgetting to loop read until EAGAIN when using edge-triggered epoll.

notes.title: select, poll and epoll
notes.html:
I/O multiplexing lets one thread block on many file descriptors at once and wake up when any is ready.

select (1983): pass three bitmaps (read, write, error) of up to FD_SETSIZE = 1024 descriptors. On return, the kernel has overwritten the bitmaps, so you rebuild them every call, and you scan all of them to find the ready ones. Cost O(n) per call, copying n entries each time.

poll: array of struct pollfd, no 1024 limit, still O(n) per call (copy the whole array to the kernel and scan it).

epoll (Linux 2.6, 2002): three calls.

  • epoll_create1() makes an epoll instance in the kernel.
  • epoll_ctl(ADD | MOD | DEL, fd, event) registers interest once. The kernel keeps a red-black tree of watched fds and a ready list.
  • epoll_wait() returns only the ready ones: cost O(ready), not O(watched).
int ep = epoll_create1(0);
struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = listen_fd };
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);
struct epoll_event ready[256];
for (;;) {
    int n = epoll_wait(ep, ready, 256, -1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) handle(ready[i].data.fd);
}

Level-triggered vs edge-triggered. Level (default): epoll_wait keeps reporting a fd as long as data remains unread. Edge (EPOLLET): reports once when data arrives; you must read until EAGAIN or you lose wake-ups. Edge reduces wake-ups but is easier to get wrong. Use EPOLLEXCLUSIVE or SO_REUSEPORT to avoid a thundering herd when several workers wait on the same listen socket.

Worked example. 10,000 connections, only 50 active at a time. select/poll: each loop copies and scans 10,000 entries, roughly 10,000 x ~20 ns = 200 microseconds of pure overhead per wake-up. epoll: returns 50 entries, about 2 microseconds. At 50,000 wake-ups per second that is 10 s of CPU per second for poll (impossible on one core) versus 0.1 s for epoll.

Platform equivalents. BSD and macOS: kqueue. Windows: IOCP (a completion model). Java NIO Selector uses epoll on Linux. Android's Looper message loop waits in native epoll_wait.

Decision gravity. Use the library (libuv, Netty, tokio, libevent) rather than raw epoll; the event-loop model forces never block the loop: one slow handler stalls every connection on that thread. Reversible at library boundary; architecture around callbacks or async/await is sticky.

Everyday analogy. A hotel front desk: instead of calling each room to ask "do you need anything?", rooms press a button and a board lights up only the ones that want service.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying epoll is "faster at I/O". It is faster at finding ready descriptors; with few, busy connections poll is just as good.
  • Doing a blocking call (DB query, Thread.sleep, big JSON parse) in an event-loop thread.
  • Forgetting epoll does not support regular files.

notes.title: The event loop in practice: why Nginx and Redis are fast
notes.html:
One thread (or one per core), no locks, never blocking, handling thousands of connections via epoll.

Nginx. A master process spawns worker processes (worker_processes auto; = one per core). Each worker runs its own event loop over thousands of connections, with a small state machine per connection (a few KB). No thread per connection, no shared locks between workers (the kernel balances accepts via SO_REUSEPORT or an accept mutex). A static file is served with sendfile (zero-copy, see below).

worker_processes auto;
events { worker_connections 20000; use epoll; }
http { sendfile on; tcp_nopush on; keepalive_timeout 30; }

With 4 workers x 20,000 connections, one box holds 80,000 concurrent connections in a few hundred MB of RAM. An Apache prefork server at 10 MB per process would need 800 GB.

Redis. Command execution is single-threaded: one thread runs an event loop (its own ae library over epoll). Why that is fast:

  • Data lives in RAM; commands are microsecond operations (GET about 1 to 2 microseconds of CPU).
  • No locks, no context switches, perfect cache locality.
  • Each command is atomic for free (no concurrent mutation of data structures).
  • The bottleneck becomes the network, about 100,000 to 200,000 ops/s on one core without pipelining, over 1 million with pipelining.

Since Redis 6, optional I/O threads (io-threads 4) parse and write sockets in parallel, while command execution stays single-threaded. Redis 8 and Valkey improved this further.

The catch: slow commands block everyone. KEYS * on 10 million keys, SMEMBERS of a huge set, or a Lua script running 50 ms stalls every client for 50 ms.

$ redis-cli --latency
min: 0, max: 1, avg: 0.12 (1832 samples)
$ redis-cli slowlog get 3
1) 1) (integer) 14
   2) (integer) 1731000000
   3) (integer) 182340        # microseconds: a 182 ms command blocked the server
   4) 1) "KEYS" 2) "*"

Use SCAN (incremental), and UNLINK instead of DEL for huge keys (frees memory in a background thread).

Industry examples. Node.js (libuv), Netty, Envoy, HAProxy, Memcached (a few threads with epoll), Vert.x, Python asyncio, Rust tokio, and Go's runtime netpoller (epoll under goroutines).

Everyday analogy. One fast chef who never waits: the chef never stands watching a pot; as soon as a timer rings they handle that dish, so one chef serves many tables. But if the chef takes a 10-minute phone call, everyone waits.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Redis is fast "because it is in memory" only. Also single-threaded design, simple data structures, and an efficient protocol (RESP).
  • Believing Redis is entirely single-threaded. Background threads exist (lazy free, AOF fsync, I/O threads in v6+).
  • Running CPU-heavy work in a Node event loop; use worker threads.

notes.title: Zero-copy I/O
notes.html:
Normal file-to-socket transfer copies data four times and crosses user/kernel boundary twice. read(file_fd, buf) then write(sock_fd, buf):

1. Disk -> kernel page cache      (DMA)
2. Page cache -> user buffer      (CPU copy)  <- wasted
3. User buffer -> socket buffer   (CPU copy)  <- wasted
4. Socket buffer -> NIC           (DMA)
Plus 2 syscalls and 2 context switches.

sendfile(out_fd, in_fd, offset, count) tells the kernel to move data directly from the page cache to the socket: no copy into user space, one syscall. With NIC scatter-gather DMA, even the copy into the socket buffer is skipped (only descriptors are passed), giving "true" zero-copy: the CPU copies zero bytes.

Related tools:

  • mmap: map a file into your address space; reads page-fault from the cache. Saves one copy, but page faults and TLB cost; error handling on truncated files is awkward (SIGBUS).
  • splice / tee: move data between a pipe and an fd inside the kernel.
  • MSG_ZEROCOPY (Linux 4.14): zero-copy send for large buffers (worth it above about 10 KB; completion notifications make it clumsy for small ones).
  • DPDK / kernel bypass / RDMA: the user program talks to the NIC directly; used in trading and some storage systems.
  • TLS caveat: encryption must read the data, so plain sendfile does not help unless kernel TLS (kTLS) is used (Nginx and Netflix's FreeBSD CDN do this).

Worked example. Serving a 1 GB video at 10 Gbit/s (1.25 GB/s). The copy path moves 1.25 GB/s through user space twice: about 2.5 GB/s of memcpy plus syscall overhead, consuming roughly one to two cores. With sendfile the CPU mostly idles; one core can fill a 10 Gbit link. Netflix Open Connect appliances serve over 100 Gbit/s per box using sendfile plus kTLS on FreeBSD (Netflix has published about 400 Gbit/s per server).

Industry examples. Kafka's consumer fetch path uses sendfile (via Java FileChannel.transferTo) so reading from disk to the consumer socket never touches the JVM heap, one reason a Kafka broker serves many consumers cheaply. Nginx sendfile on;. Apache EnableSendfile.

Decision gravity. Use sendfile for static content and log streaming without transformation; once you must modify data (compress, encrypt in user space), it no longer applies. Reversible config.

Everyday analogy. Instead of a courier carrying a parcel into your office and then to the post box, the post-room hands the parcel straight to the post van.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming zero-copy means no copies at all. The DMA transfers still happen; it means zero CPU copies between user and kernel.
  • Forgetting TLS and compression defeat the plain sendfile path.

notes.title: io_uring
notes.html:
io_uring (Linux 5.1, 2019, by Jens Axboe) is a true asynchronous I/O interface built on two shared ring buffers between user space and kernel. You write requests into the submission queue (SQ); the kernel writes results into the completion queue (CQ). Because the rings are shared memory, you can submit many operations and collect many completions with zero or one syscalls (io_uring_enter), or even zero syscalls with SQPOLL (a kernel thread polls the SQ).

// liburing sketch: read 4 KB asynchronously
struct io_uring ring; io_uring_queue_init(256, &ring, 0);
struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, buf, 4096, 0);
sqe->user_data = 42;
io_uring_submit(&ring);                     // one syscall for many sqes
struct io_uring_cqe *cqe; io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
printf("req %llu result %d\n", cqe->user_data, cqe->res);
io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);

What it adds over epoll:

  • Real async disk I/O. epoll cannot wait on regular files; Linux's older AIO (libaio) only worked well with O_DIRECT. io_uring handles buffered files, sockets, accept, connect, send, recv, fsync, openat and more through one interface.
  • Batching: 32 operations, one syscall.
  • Fixed files and fixed buffers: pre-register fds and buffers to skip per-call lookups.
  • Linked operations: "read then write then fsync" as a chain.
  • Multishot accept/recv, provided buffers, and since 6.x, zero-copy send/receive.

Worked example. A storage service doing 1 million 4 KB random reads/s on NVMe. With blocking pread per thread you need many threads and ~1 million syscalls/s (about 0.3 s of CPU in syscall entry/exit alone, more with KPTI mitigations). With io_uring batching 64 at a time: ~16,000 submits/s, and SQPOLL can bring it to near zero. Reported results show single-core NVMe IOPS rising from ~400K to over a million.

Trade-offs and security. It is a big, young kernel attack surface: many container runtimes and Google (for ChromeOS and production) restricted or disabled io_uring after multiple privilege-escalation CVEs; Docker's default seccomp profile blocks it in newer releases (confirm for your version). Needs kernel 5.10+ for sane feature sets, 6.x for the newest ops. Programming model is more complex than epoll.

Industry examples. RocksDB and some databases experimented with it; ScyllaDB's Seastar has an io_uring backend; Rust runtimes (tokio-uring, glommio, monoio) and the liburing library; Node's libuv uses it for file ops in newer versions (confirm per release). Cloudflare, Meta have written about using it selectively.

Decision gravity. Choose io_uring when you need async disk I/O or extremely high syscall rates and control your kernel version; epoll remains the safe default for ordinary network servers. Medium reversibility: adds a platform dependency (Linux only).

Everyday analogy. Instead of phoning the kitchen for each order, you drop a stack of order slips on a shared counter and pick up finished plates from a second counter, without speaking.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying io_uring is just a faster epoll. It is a completion-based async interface, different in kind.
  • Ignoring the security posture (seccomp/blocked in many sandboxes).
  • Claiming epoll supports disk files.

notes.title: Choosing an I/O model and debugging it
notes.html:
Decision ladder.

Situation Choice
Under about 2,000 concurrent connections, simple team Blocking threads
Same code style, huge concurrency Virtual threads (Java 21) or goroutines
10K to 1M connections, mostly idle Event loop on epoll (Netty, Node, Nginx)
Heavy disk I/O async, newest kernels io_uring
Serving big static files sendfile (plus kTLS)
CPU-bound work in an event-driven server Hand off to a worker pool

Debugging toolkit (Linux).

$ ss -s                                   # socket totals
Total: 41234  TCP: 40112 (estab 38990, closed 120, timewait 118)
$ ss -ltn                                 # Recv-Q on a LISTEN socket = accept backlog waiting
State   Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port
LISTEN  129     128     0.0.0.0:8080      # Recv-Q > Send-Q: accept queue FULL, app too slow
$ sudo strace -f -c -p 2310 -- sleep 5    # which syscalls dominate
% time  seconds  calls  syscall
 71.2   2.9      90210  epoll_wait
 20.1   0.8     310550  write
$ cat /proc/2310/limits | grep 'open files'
Max open files   1024   1048576   files      # raise nofile limit for C10K

Production patterns:

  • "Too many open files" (EMFILE): ulimit -n / LimitNOFILE=1048576 in systemd; one fd per socket.
  • Accept queue overflow: ss -ltn shows Recv-Q at the backlog (somaxconn, default 4096 on newer kernels, 128 on older). Symptom: clients see connect timeouts while CPU is idle. nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows counts drops.
  • Event loop lag: one thread at 100% CPU (top -H) while others idle; latency across all connections rises. Find the blocking handler with perf top or an application profiler.
  • Ephemeral port exhaustion on the client side: 28K ports by default (net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range), many TIME_WAIT; use connection pooling and keep-alive.

Everyday analogy. A busy restaurant: check how many diners are queuing at the door (accept queue), whether the single chef is stuck (loop lag), and whether you ran out of table numbers (fds).

Common interview traps.

  • Raising thread pool sizes instead of finding the blocking call.
  • Not knowing where the connection backlog is visible (ss -ltn).
  • Treating the default ulimit -n 1024 as fine for a server.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• I/O is slow compared to CPU; the I/O model decides what a thread does while waiting. Little's law: concurrency = throughput x latency.
  • Blocking + thread per connection is simplest; costs memory and context switches at C10K scale. Virtual threads and goroutines bring the model back cheaply.
  • Non-blocking returns EAGAIN; useless alone and does nothing for regular files.
  • select/poll are O(n) per call; epoll registers once and returns only ready fds. Level vs edge triggering; use SO_REUSEPORT or exclusive wake-ups.
  • Nginx (worker per core, event loop, sendfile) and Redis (single-threaded in-memory, no locks, atomic commands) are fast because of event loops plus no blocking; a slow command blocks everyone.
  • Zero-copy (sendfile, splice, MSG_ZEROCOPY) avoids CPU copies; TLS and transformation defeat the simple version unless kTLS is used.
  • io_uring is shared-ring async I/O for files and sockets with batching; powerful but young and often blocked in sandboxes.
  • Debug with ss -ltn, strace -c, top -H, fd limits and accept-queue counters.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between blocking, non-blocking and asynchronous I/O?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most candidates use "async" and "non-blocking" as synonyms. Getting this right shows you understand who does the waiting and who does the work.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With blocking I/O my thread sleeps inside the call until the data is there. With non-blocking I/O the call returns immediately with "not ready" (EAGAIN) and I have to come back and ask again. With asynchronous I/O I submit the whole operation, keep working, and the kernel tells me when it is complete and the data is already in my buffer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A CPU does a billion steps a second; a same-datacentre round trip is about 500 microseconds, which is 500,000 idle cycles. So the question is always: what does the thread do while it waits?

Model            Who waits?         Call returns when        Typical API
Blocking         my thread (asleep) data is ready & copied   read()
Non-blocking     nobody, I poll     immediately, maybe EAGAIN read() + O_NONBLOCK
Multiplexing     my thread, on MANY select/poll/epoll_wait returns when ANY fd ready
Async (completion) nobody           op submitted; result later io_uring, Windows IOCP

The key split: in readiness models (non-blocking, epoll) the kernel says "you may now read without blocking" and YOU do the copy. In completion models (io_uring, IOCP) the kernel does the operation and says "it is done". Stevens' five classic models are blocking, non-blocking, multiplexing, signal-driven and async.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying epoll is asynchronous I/O. It is readiness notification; the read itself is still a synchronous call.
  • Saying a blocking thread burns CPU. It sleeps; the cost is memory and scheduling.
  • Thinking O_NONBLOCK works on regular files. Disk files are always "ready", so it does nothing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Node.js async? -> The API is callback/promise based on top of epoll (readiness) plus a thread pool for file I/O; JS code itself runs on one thread.
  2. Why can epoll not wait on a disk file? -> Regular files are always reported ready; the read may still sleep on a page-cache miss.
  3. Which is "true" async on Linux? -> io_uring (and old libaio with O_DIRECT); epoll is not.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer lists the definitions. A senior distinguishes readiness from completion, names the APIs, and notes that file I/O needs a thread pool or io_uring.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Node service stalled on large file reads because fs.readFileSync blocked the single loop; the team assumed "non-blocking" meant nothing could block.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a thread-per-connection server struggle at 10,000 connections, even though sleeping threads use no CPU?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the real cost is memory and scheduling, not CPU spin.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A blocked thread does not burn CPU, but each one holds a stack (Java defaults to 1 MB virtual) plus kernel structures, and the scheduler has to track thousands of entities. At 10,000 threads that is gigabytes of address space, 100+ MB real memory, rising context switches and poor cache locality. An event loop uses one thread for all of them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per thread: user stack reservation (1 MB Java, 8 MB default C main thread), kernel stack plus task struct (about 10 KB), TLB and cache pollution on every switch. A context switch costs 2 to 5 microseconds directly and more through cache misses.

10,000 threads x 1 MB stack  = ~10 GB virtual
10,000 threads x ~100 KB real = ~1 GB resident (stack pages touched + kernel)
If 2,000 become runnable at once -> thousands of switches per ms, cache thrash

This was the C10K problem (Kegel, 1999). The fix was cheap per-connection state plus epoll. Today Java 21 virtual threads and Go goroutines bring the blocking style back: the runtime parks the lightweight thread and uses epoll underneath.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing a pool for I/O-bound work by core count. The formula is roughly cores x (1 + wait/compute).
  • Assuming more threads = more throughput. Past saturation, switching overhead lowers it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is thread-per-connection still the right choice? -> Below a few thousand connections; it is simplest to write and debug.
  2. How do virtual threads change this? -> Cheap (KB), parked on blocking calls; same code, event-loop scale, but pinning (synchronized, native calls) can still hurt.
  3. What limits the thread count on Linux? -> ulimit -u, kernel.threads-max, vm.max_map_count, cgroup pids.max, and memory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "threads are heavy". Senior: quantifies stack and kernel cost, names the scheduler/cache effect, and ties it to virtual threads as the modern answer.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat gateway moved from 200 pooled threads to Netty after hitting OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread at around 30k sockets.

questions.contextHtml:
A Spring Boot service runs on 4 vCPUs with the Tomcat default of 200 worker threads. Normally each request calls a database for 100 ms. Peak traffic is 1,500 req/s. At 15:10 the DB gets slow (1 s per query). The dashboard shows:

CPU:            12%
tomcat.threads.busy: 200/200
http p99:       9.8 s
requests/s:     198
DB CPU:         95%

Someone proposes raising CPU to 16 vCPUs.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what is happening and what you would do.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale up the box." CPU is 12%; more cores change nothing because threads are asleep waiting on the DB. They also miss that the DB is the real problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the DB slow down first or traffic grow first (direction of causality)? Is there a connection pool limit smaller than 200 (that would be the true cap)? Are there timeouts on the DB call? Is the accept queue full?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load or fail fast: lower DB call timeout to 2 s, enable a circuit breaker, serve cached data for read endpoints. Do not add threads, that just sends more queries to a saturated DB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) DB saturated (bad query or lock) so latency jumped; (b) pool of 200 threads is capped by Little's law; (c) connection pool misconfigured; (d) GC pause red herring, CPU is low.
  4. How I'd verify: Little's law: concurrency 200 = throughput x latency, so 200 / 1 s = 200 req/s, matches the dashboard exactly. jstack shows 200 threads in SocketInputStream.read or the pool's getConnection. Check DB pg_stat_activity for slow queries.
  5. Root cause: Capacity of a blocking pool = pool size / latency. At 100 ms it capped at 2,000 req/s; at 1 s it caps at 200 req/s and the rest queue. The pool turned a slow dependency into a full outage.
  6. Fix: Short term: fix the slow query, add timeouts, bulkhead per dependency. Long term: separate pools per downstream, consider virtual threads so the pool is no longer the cap (the DB pool then becomes the limiter, which is desired).
  7. Prevention: Alert on busy threads/200, on p99 of each downstream call, and on pool wait time. Load test with an injected 1 s dependency delay.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise the thread count blindly: 2,000 threads would push 2,000 concurrent queries into an already saturated DB and make it worse.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the DB is healthy but a third-party API is slow? -> Same arithmetic; use a dedicated bulkhead pool and a timeout so it cannot starve the rest.
  • Would virtual threads fix it? -> They remove the thread cap, but the DB connection pool and the DB itself remain limits; you must keep a concurrency limiter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added 4x more app nodes during a slow-DB incident. Each node opened 200 more connections and the DB fell over completely. The real fix was one missing index.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests more CPU or restarts; cannot explain why CPU is low.
  • Hire: applies Little's law, identifies the DB, adds timeouts and a circuit breaker.
  • Strong hire: also bulkheads, warns against scaling out into a saturated DB, and proposes alerting on saturation of the pool.

questions.promptHtml: How do select, poll and epoll differ, and why does epoll scale better?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic systems question; separates people who memorised "epoll is faster" from those who know why.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: select and poll make me hand the kernel the whole list of descriptors on every call, and then I scan the whole list to find the ready ones, so each wake-up is O(n). select is also limited to 1024 fds. epoll lets me register each fd once in a kernel structure and epoll_wait returns only the ready ones, so the cost is O(ready), not O(watched).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
select : 3 bitmaps, FD_SETSIZE=1024, kernel overwrites them -> rebuild + scan every call
poll   : array of struct pollfd, no 1024 limit, still copy + scan O(n) every call
epoll  : epoll_create1 -> epoll_ctl(ADD/MOD/DEL) once -> epoll_wait returns ready list
         kernel keeps a red-black tree of watched fds and a ready list

Worked numbers: 10,000 connections, 50 active. poll copies and scans 10,000 entries (about 200 microseconds) per wake-up; epoll returns 50 (about 2 microseconds). At 50,000 wake-ups/s that is 10 s of CPU per second for poll versus 0.1 s for epoll. With few, busy connections poll is just as good. BSD/macOS use kqueue, Windows uses IOCP.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
int ep = epoll_create1(0);
epoll_event ev{}; ev.events = EPOLLIN; ev.data.fd = listen_fd;
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);
epoll_event ready[256];
for (;;) {
    int n = epoll_wait(ep, ready, 256, -1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) handle(ready[i].data.fd);
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "epoll is faster at I/O." It is faster at finding ready fds.
  • Forgetting epoll cannot watch regular files.
  • Writing raw epoll in application code instead of using libuv/Netty/tokio.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Level vs edge triggered? -> Level re-reports while data is unread; edge reports once, so you must read until EAGAIN.
  2. Thundering herd on a shared listen socket? -> EPOLLEXCLUSIVE or SO_REUSEPORT with one listener per worker.
  3. Does Java NIO use epoll? -> Yes, Selector is epoll on Linux.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "epoll is O(1)". Senior: O(ready) vs O(watched), copy cost per call, edge-trigger pitfalls, and when poll is just as good.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A proxy using poll() with 40k idle connections burned a full core in sys_poll; the switch to epoll dropped that to under 2%.

questions.contextHtml:
A custom TCP proxy uses edge-triggered epoll for performance. Under light load it works. Under load testing, some clients hang forever even though they sent complete requests; the server shows sockets in ESTABLISHED with Recv-Q of several KB on ss. CPU is idle.

epoll_event ev{}; ev.events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLET; ev.data.fd = cfd;
epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, cfd, &ev);

void on_readable(int fd) {
    char buf[4096];
    ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);   // fd is non-blocking
    if (n > 0) process(buf, n);
}

A red herring: the team suspects a kernel bug because it "only fails at high throughput".

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the buffer" or "switch to level-triggered without knowing why". They miss that edge-triggered fires once per new data arrival.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the fd non-blocking? Is the client sending more than 4 KB per request? Does it recover when the client sends another byte (that would confirm lost edge)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Switch to level-triggered (drop EPOLLET) as a hotfix; it re-reports until data is drained.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) read once instead of draining to EAGAIN; (b) lost accept edges for the listener, same cause; (c) buffer sizing, which only changes where it breaks.
  4. How I'd verify: ss -tn shows Recv-Q greater than 0 with no wake-ups; strace -p shows no epoll_wait return for that fd; sending an extra byte from the client unblocks it.
  5. Root cause: An edge is reported when new data arrives, not while data remains. A request larger than 4 KB leaves unread bytes in the socket buffer; no new edge fires, so the fd is never reported again.
  6. Fix:
void on_readable(int fd) {
    for (;;) {
        ssize_t n = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
        if (n > 0) { process(buf, n); continue; }
        if (n < 0 && errno == EAGAIN) break;   // drained
        if (n == 0 || errno != EINTR) { close(fd); break; }
    }
}

Same rule for accept (loop until EAGAIN). Add a per-fd fairness budget so one busy client cannot starve others. 7. Prevention: A test sending payloads larger than the buffer; a lint/review rule "ET requires read-until-EAGAIN"; prefer a library. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Level-triggered is safer and the wake-up saving of ET is small for most workloads; I would not claim ET is always better.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What about writes? -> With ET, write until EAGAIN, then register for EPOLLOUT only when a send buffer is full.
  • Why not just read a huge buffer once? -> Any size can be exceeded; the loop is the correct invariant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A proxy dropped roughly 1 in 10,000 large uploads. It took a week because small test payloads never exceeded one read.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the kernel or the buffer size.
  • Hire: identifies read-once under ET and fixes with a drain loop.
  • Strong hire: also covers accept, writes, fairness, and explains why level-triggered is a valid hotfix.

questions.promptHtml: Redis executes commands on a single thread. Why is it still so fast, and what is the catch?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about locks, cache locality and event loops instead of repeating "it is in memory".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Commands are microsecond operations on in-memory structures, and one thread driving an epoll loop needs no locks, has no context switches, keeps caches warm, and gets atomic commands for free. The bottleneck becomes the network, not the CPU. The catch is that any slow command blocks every client, such as KEYS * or a big SMEMBERS.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Redis uses its own ae event library over epoll. One GET costs about 1 to 2 microseconds of CPU, so one core serves 100,000 to 200,000 ops/s without pipelining and over a million with pipelining. Since Redis 6, optional I/O threads parse and write sockets in parallel but command execution stays single-threaded. Background threads still exist for lazy free (UNLINK), AOF fsync and so on.

Client 1 \
Client 2  -> epoll -> one thread: read -> execute -> write -> next
Client 3 /
A 50 ms command = 50 ms of stall for ALL clients.
$ redis-cli slowlog get 1
1) 1) (integer) 14
   3) (integer) 182340      # microseconds: a 182 ms command blocked the server
   4) 1) "KEYS" 2) "*"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fast only because in-memory": also design, simple structures, RESP protocol.
  • "Entirely single-threaded": background and I/O threads exist.
  • Using DEL on a huge key instead of UNLINK; KEYS instead of SCAN.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you use more cores? -> Redis Cluster / multiple instances sharded, or I/O threads for network work.
  2. Why is MULTI/EXEC atomic? -> Single executor, nothing interleaves.
  3. A fork for RDB: any risk? -> Copy-on-write can double memory under heavy writes; keep headroom.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "memory is fast". Senior: lock-free, no switches, the event loop contract (never block it), and a plan for slow commands.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A KEYS user:* in a debug script froze a cache shared by 40 services for 400 ms and tripped timeouts everywhere.

questions.contextHtml:
A shared Redis (one primary, 6 GB dataset, 20k ops/s) is used by 30 services. Every few minutes all clients see a latency spike to 300 ms, then it recovers. Redis CPU on the core shows 100% during the spike; network and memory look fine. Excerpts:

$ redis-cli --latency
min: 0, max: 312, avg: 0.9
$ redis-cli slowlog get 2
1) 1) (integer) 207  3) (integer) 298114  4) 1) "SMEMBERS" 2) "feed:global"
2) 1) (integer) 206  3) (integer) 41200   4) 1) "KEYS" 2) "session:*"
$ redis-cli scard feed:global
(integer) 4800000

Red herring: the hosting team points to a noisy neighbour (st is 0.2%).
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without taking the cache down.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a replica" or "increase memory". Replicas do not help a command that blocks the primary and reads from replicas would just move the pain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which service issues SMEMBERS feed:global and how often? Is latency-monitor enabled? Do clients share one connection pool?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Find the caller from CLIENT LIST / slowlog client info and stop or throttle it; rename/disable KEYS via ACL.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) O(N) commands on a 4.8M member set; (b) KEYS pattern scans; (c) fork for RDB (check latest_fork_usec); (d) noisy neighbour, ruled out by st.
  4. How I'd verify: SLOWLOG GET, LATENCY DOCTOR, INFO commandstats (usec_per_call), INFO persistence for fork time.
  5. Root cause: Single-threaded execution means one 298 ms SMEMBERS stalls every client. CPU 100% on one core is the symptom of the loop being busy, not of load.
  6. Fix: Short term: ACL deny KEYS, SMEMBERS on huge sets from the app. Long term: use SSCAN with count, or shard the set into buckets (feed:global:{0..255}), UNLINK for deletes, and ACL/rename-command guardrails.
  7. Prevention: Alert on slowlog growth and instantaneous_ops_per_sec drops; review rule for O(N) commands; a separate instance for noisy workloads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise slowlog-log-slower-than. I would not move to a bigger instance since single-thread speed is the limit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the app must read the whole set? -> Paginate with SSCAN, cache a snapshot, or move that data to a database better at scans.
  • How do you protect against future abuse? -> Per-service ACL and a dedicated instance for heavy workloads.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" admin dashboard called HGETALL on a 200 MB hash every 10 seconds and caused hourly mystery latency for a year.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the network or scales hardware.
  • Hire: reads the slowlog, ties it to the single thread, uses SSCAN/UNLINK.
  • Strong hire: sharding keys, ACL guardrails, workload isolation and alerting.

questions.contextHtml:
A media service serves 800 MB video files from local NVMe over plain HTTP from a custom Java server using FileInputStream.read(buf) then socket.write(buf) with an 8 KB buffer. One box has a 10 Gbit NIC and 16 cores. At 6 Gbit/s the box is at 85% CPU, mostly in the app and kernel; the NIC is not saturated. perf top shows:

 31%  [kernel]  copy_user_enhanced_fast_string
 18%  [kernel]  tcp_sendmsg
 11%  libjvm.so  (JNI copy to/from heap)

Management wants to double throughput without buying hardware. Someone suggests more threads.
questions.promptHtml: What would you change and what are the limits?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add threads or a bigger buffer." The CPU is spent copying bytes, so parallelism only moves the problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is traffic TLS or plain? Do we transform data (compress, watermark)? Are files hot in page cache or cold? Is the JVM heap being touched per byte?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed, it is optimisation; but cap concurrent downloads so latency for other traffic stays fine.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) two CPU copies per byte (page cache to user buffer, then to socket buffer) plus the JNI heap copy; (b) small buffer means many syscalls; (c) TLS cost if present; (d) NIC, ruled out.
  4. How I'd verify: perf top (as above), strace -c showing millions of read/write, vmstat sy share.
  5. Root cause: Each byte crosses the user/kernel boundary twice and is copied by the CPU twice. At 6 Gbit/s (750 MB/s) that is 1.5 GB/s of memcpy and about 190,000 syscalls/s at 8 KB.
  6. Fix: Use FileChannel.transferTo (sendfile) or put Nginx in front with sendfile on; tcp_nopush on;. Data goes page cache to NIC; with scatter-gather DMA the CPU copies zero bytes. If TLS is required, use kernel TLS (kTLS) with sendfile, or terminate TLS at a layer that supports it; otherwise expect crypto cost to dominate. Use ulimit and tune socket buffers.
try (FileChannel ch = FileChannel.open(path)) {
    long pos = 0, size = ch.size();
    while (pos < size) pos += ch.transferTo(pos, size - pos, socketChannel);
}
  1. Prevention: Benchmark with representative files; track CPU per Gbit/s; alert on sy and copy functions in profiles.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Zero-copy does not apply once I must modify bytes (compression, user-space TLS). I would not use mmap for huge files: page faults, TLB cost and SIGBUS on truncation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cold files on HDD? -> Disk becomes the limit; sendfile still avoids copies but readahead and IO scheduling matter.
  • Does sendfile help for small responses? -> Marginally; header building and syscall count dominate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Switching a log-shipping tool from read/write to sendfile cut CPU from 40% to 8% on a 10 Gbit link; the real surprise was that enabling TLS brought most of it back until kTLS was used.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more threads or hardware.
  • Hire: identifies copies and moves to sendfile/transferTo.
  • Strong hire: calls out TLS/compression limits, kTLS, page cache behaviour, and measures with perf.

questions.promptHtml: What does "zero-copy" actually mean for sendfile, and how many copies happen in a normal read-then-write file transfer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many say "zero-copy means no copying". The signal is whether you can count copies and context switches.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A normal read then write copies data four times: DMA disk to page cache, CPU copy to my buffer, CPU copy to the socket buffer, DMA to the NIC, with two syscalls and two mode switches. sendfile lets the kernel move data from page cache to socket without it entering user space. "Zero-copy" means zero CPU copies between user and kernel; DMA transfers still happen.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
read+write:                       sendfile:
1 disk -> page cache  (DMA)       1 disk -> page cache (DMA)
2 cache -> user buf   (CPU) x     2 (skipped; with SG-DMA only descriptors go
3 user buf -> sock buf (CPU) x        to the socket buffer)
4 sock buf -> NIC     (DMA)       3 page cache -> NIC (DMA)
2 syscalls, 2 mode switches       1 syscall

Related primitives: mmap (saves one copy but page faults and SIGBUS), splice/tee (pipe to fd in kernel), MSG_ZEROCOPY (Linux 4.14, worth it above roughly 10 KB, completion notifications are clumsy), DPDK/RDMA (kernel bypass). Kafka's consumer fetch path uses transferTo, so data never touches the JVM heap. Nginx sendfile on;.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming no copies at all happen.
  • Forgetting TLS and compression need to read the bytes, which defeats plain sendfile (kTLS is the exception).
  • Using mmap as a universal zero-copy answer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does TLS break it? -> Encryption needs plaintext in the CPU; user-space TLS must read the file. kTLS moves the cipher into the kernel.
  2. When would you not use sendfile? -> When you transform data or serve tiny responses.
  3. What is the page cache's role? -> Source of the data; a cold file still needs the DMA from disk first.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "avoids copying to user space". Senior: counts four copies, distinguishes CPU from DMA, knows SG-DMA, TLS/kTLS and the Kafka example.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Kafka brokers serve many consumers cheaply because of sendfile; enabling TLS on brokers brought CPU up sharply because that path was lost.

questions.contextHtml:
After a marketing push, a Node/Express API behind a load balancer sees clients timing out on connect (3 s). The app node shows CPU 35%, memory fine, p50 latency of served requests is 20 ms. The LB reports many connect failures to this node. On the node:

$ ss -ltn
State   Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port
LISTEN  512     511     0.0.0.0:3000
$ nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows TcpExtListenDrops
TcpExtListenOverflows   48210
TcpExtListenDrops       48210
$ top -H -p $(pgrep node)
 PID  %CPU COMMAND
 2310  99.0 node          <- the main thread
 2318   4.0 node (libuv workers)
$ cat /proc/sys/net/core/somaxconn
128

Red herring: an engineer notes "only 35% CPU, so we have headroom".
questions.promptHtml: Why are clients failing and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "CPU is only 35% so it is a network issue", missing that 35% is averaged across cores while the single event-loop thread is at 99%.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many cores, and how many Node processes? Is there a cluster/PM2 setup? What was the traffic change? Are requests CPU-heavy (JSON, crypto)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add nodes behind the LB or restart with more worker processes; raise somaxconn and the listen backlog as a stopgap; shed load at the LB.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) event loop saturated on one core so accept() is slow; (b) backlog min(listen, somaxconn)=128 is small; (c) a blocking call in a handler; (d) SYN flood (check SYN cookies, unlikely given real traffic).
  4. How I'd verify: ss -ltn Recv-Q equal to backlog means accept queue is full; nstat ListenOverflows increments; top -H shows one thread pegged; a CPU profile or --prof flame graph finds the handler.
  5. Root cause: One thread cannot accept and serve fast enough. The kernel queues completed handshakes in the accept queue (size min(backlog, somaxconn)); when it is full, new connections are dropped or the SYN-ACK is ignored, and clients retry after 1 s, 3 s so connects time out while the CPU average looks idle.
  6. Fix: Short term: run one process per core (cluster/PM2, or SO_REUSEPORT with multiple listeners), raise backlog and somaxconn (4096+), also tcp_max_syn_backlog. Long term: profile and remove CPU hot spots in the loop, offload heavy work to worker threads, autoscale on event-loop lag not average CPU.
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096
# app: server.listen({ port: 3000, backlog: 4096 })
  1. Prevention: Alert on ListenOverflows, per-core CPU, event-loop lag (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay), and Recv-Q on listeners.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Raising the backlog only hides the problem and increases queueing latency; I would not rely on it alone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why do clients see exactly 1 s/3 s delays? -> SYN retransmit timers after a dropped handshake.
  • Could tcp_abort_on_overflow help? -> It sends RST instead of silently dropping so clients fail fast; useful with an LB retry policy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-day 20x spike hit a single-process service on a 32-core host. Dashboards showed 3% CPU while one core was pinned and 40% of connects were dropped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: trusts average CPU and blames the network.
  • Hire: finds the accept queue overflow and the saturated single thread.
  • Strong hire: explains the queue arithmetic, retransmit timings, per-core metrics, and multi-process or reuseport design.

questions.promptHtml: How is io_uring different from epoll, and when would you actually adopt it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth on modern Linux I/O and judgment about adopting young technology.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: epoll tells me a socket is ready and then I make the syscall to do the read. io_uring is completion-based: I put requests in a shared submission ring, the kernel performs them, and results appear in a completion ring, so I can batch dozens of operations per syscall, or none with SQPOLL. It also does real async file I/O, which epoll cannot. I would adopt it for heavy disk I/O or extreme syscall rates on kernels I control; epoll remains the default for ordinary network servers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
epoll:     wait -> "fd 7 ready" -> read(7) syscall -> process        (1 syscall per op)
io_uring:  fill SQEs (read, recv, accept, fsync...) -> 1 enter -> CQEs back  (batched)

Features: fixed files/buffers (skip per-call lookups), linked operations (read then write then fsync), multishot accept/recv, provided buffers, newer zero-copy send. Numbers (verify for your kernel): millions of 4 KB NVMe reads per core versus around 400K with blocking pread. Security: a large, young attack surface; Google and several container runtimes restrict or disable it, and Docker's default seccomp blocks it in newer versions (confirm for yours). Needs 5.10+ for a sane feature set. Linux only.

io_uring ring; io_uring_queue_init(256, &ring, 0);
io_uring_sqe* sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, buf, 4096, 0);
io_uring_submit(&ring);
io_uring_cqe* cqe; io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "A faster epoll": it is different in kind (completion vs readiness).
  • Ignoring the seccomp/sandbox posture.
  • Believing epoll handles disk files.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does SQPOLL cost? -> A kernel thread spinning on the SQ; burns a core for near-zero syscalls.
  2. Why not libaio? -> Only worked well with O_DIRECT and covers few operation types.
  3. Where is it used? -> Seastar, glommio, tokio-uring, some storage engines; libuv uses it selectively (verify per release).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "newer and faster". Senior: readiness vs completion, batching math, file I/O gap, security and kernel-version constraints.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team enabled io_uring in a database and then found their container platform's seccomp profile blocked it in staging; they needed an epoll fallback.

questions.contextHtml:
A Node.js service reads uploaded CSV files (up to 200 MB) from local disk, parses them and streams results. The team believes "everything is non-blocking". During report generation, health checks from the LB time out (2 s) and the whole instance flaps. Metrics:

event loop delay p99:     3.4 s
CPU (main thread):        100%
libuv threadpool queue:   128 pending fs ops
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE:       default (4)

Code snippet in the handler:

const txt = fs.readFileSync(path, "utf8");   // used "for simplicity"
const rows = JSON.parse(convert(txt));       // 150 MB string
await Promise.all(files.map(f => fs.promises.readFile(f)));  // 500 files
questions.promptHtml: Explain every way this blocks and redesign it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it async with promises." Promises do not add parallelism; the parse still runs on the loop and the fs promises still compete for four threads.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the health check share the same process? How often do reports run? Can the work be moved to a queue?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move report generation to a separate worker deployment so health checks and user traffic stay isolated; raise the LB timeout only temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) readFileSync and JSON.parse of a 150 MB string block the loop (CPU-bound on the main thread); (b) 500 parallel readFile calls saturate the 4-thread libuv pool, starving DNS lookups, crypto, zlib which share it; (c) memory pressure causing GC pauses.
  4. How I'd verify: monitorEventLoopDelay, clinic doctor / --cpu-prof flame graph, top -H showing a hot main thread, strace -f -e trace=read for sync reads.
  5. Root cause: Regular files cannot be polled with epoll (always "ready"), so Node uses a thread pool for file I/O; that pool is small and shared. Parsing and *Sync calls run on the loop thread, so while they run no connection is serviced, including the health check.
  6. Fix: Stream with fs.createReadStream and an incremental parser; run CPU work in worker_threads (or a separate service); cap concurrency with a limiter (for example 8 files at a time); set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to a measured value; use a job queue for reports.
  7. Prevention: Ban *Sync in request paths via lint rule, alert on loop delay p99, load test with large payloads.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not simply raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 128: it helps I/O parallelism but not the parse, and extra threads add memory and contention.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is DNS slow during this? -> getaddrinfo uses the same libuv pool.
  • Could io_uring help? -> For file reads possibly, but the CPU-bound parse remains.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "quick" synchronous config reload on each request cost 8 ms; at 500 rps it consumed 4 cores' worth of loop time on one thread, and p99 collapsed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds async/await and calls it done.
  • Hire: separates CPU blocking from I/O, uses streams and workers.
  • Strong hire: knows the shared libuv pool, regular-file epoll limit, isolation of health checks, and concurrency limits.

questions.contextHtml: A Java 17 payment-notification service uses Tomcat with 400 threads. Each request fans out to 3 slow partner APIs (each p50 300 ms, p99 4 s). Traffic is doubling to 6,000 req/s in three months. Today at 3,000 req/s the pool is often exhausted; heap is 4 GB, 400 threads. The team has three options: (A) migrate to Netty/WebFlux, (B) upgrade to Java 21 and enable virtual threads, (C) keep threads and shard to 4x more nodes. The code base is 250k lines of blocking JDBC and Spring MVC.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you pick and how do you migrate with live traffic?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reactive is always faster, rewrite everything." Ignores cost, JDBC blocking, debugging difficulty and team risk.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does the time go (partner I/O vs DB vs CPU)? Is JDBC on the hot path? Can we upgrade the JDK in this timeframe? What is the SLO and the cost budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add per-partner timeouts, bulkheads and a circuit breaker, so a 4 s p99 partner cannot hold threads; this is needed regardless of the option.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) threads are idle waiting on partners, so a cheap-blocking model is the right fit; (b) WebFlux needs non-blocking drivers for everything or it will block the loop; (c) scaling out is the quick but costly path.
  4. How I'd verify: Little's law: 6,000 req/s x ~1.5 s average fan-out wait gives about 9,000 concurrent requests, far above 400 threads. Thread dumps show blocked in socket read. Check JDK 21 pinning (-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads).
  5. Root cause: The concurrency required is dictated by throughput x latency, and the blocking model charges ~1 MB of stack per concurrent request.
  6. Fix: Pick B. Virtual threads keep the blocking code and stack traces, park cheaply on socket reads (epoll underneath), and scale to tens of thousands of concurrent requests. Roll out by canary: one node pool on Java 21 behind the LB at 5%, then 25%, 100%. Replace synchronized blocks around I/O with ReentrantLock to avoid pinning, and keep a semaphore on the JDBC pool (virtual threads do not make the DB faster).
// Spring Boot 3.2+
// spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
  1. Prevention: Metrics for concurrency per dependency, pinned-thread monitoring, load test at 2x target.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rewrite to WebFlux unless the team has the skills; it is a one-way door, makes debugging harder, and JDBC would still block. I would not just shard (C) since it multiplies cost without removing the cap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the company is stuck on Java 17? -> Short term bulkheads and more nodes; a Netty-based async client only for the partner fan-out.
  • ThreadLocal usage? -> Virtual threads support them but millions of virtual threads with big ThreadLocals use memory; review.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team moved a fan-out gateway to virtual threads and cut nodes from 24 to 8, but a synchronized HTTP client wrapper pinned carriers until it was replaced.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by hype, no capacity math.
  • Hire: uses Little's law and recommends virtual threads or async with reasons.
  • Strong hire: staged migration, pinning, JDBC and DB limits, bulkheads, and cost comparison.

questions.contextHtml:
A push-notification gateway holds 100,000 idle long-lived WebSocket connections per node today (one Netty event loop group). Product wants 10x connections on the same fleet size ("let each node hold 1M"). Average 1 message per connection per 5 minutes. At 100k connections the node shows:

RSS 7.2 GB   fds 100,312 / limit 1,048,576
CPU 6%       ss -s: estab 99810, timewait 8
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999   (the node is a server, not a client)
Recv-Q/Send-Q kernel buffers: ~ 40 KB avg per socket

A peer says "TCP port limit of 65,535 means you cannot go above 65k connections."
questions.promptHtml: Is 1M feasible on one node? What breaks first and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Repeats the 65k port myth or says "just add RAM" without per-connection accounting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is TLS terminated on the node? What is the failure blast radius when a node dies (reconnect storm of 1M)? Message fan-out pattern? Is the NIC/LB able to hold 1M flows?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (planning); but protect against reconnect storms with jittered backoff.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) memory per connection (7.2 GB / 100k = 72 KB) means 72 GB at 1M; (b) kernel socket buffers and TLS state; (c) fd limits and conntrack tables; (d) ports are not a server limit because the 4-tuple differs by client IP/port.
  4. How I'd verify: /proc/net/sockstat, smem, ss -tm for buffer use, nf_conntrack_count, a synthetic 1M-connection load test with multiple client IPs.
  5. Root cause (what limits): Not ports (the server listens on one port; uniqueness is the 4-tuple), not CPU (6% idle-mostly). The limits are memory per connection, fds, conntrack and thundering reconnects.
  6. Fix: Cut per-socket memory: smaller tcp_rmem/tcp_wmem defaults (for idle sockets), pooled/shared buffers in Netty, avoid per-connection thread-locals, TLS session size awareness (about 20-40 KB each). Raise nofile (set LimitNOFILE=2097152, fs.nr_open), tune conntrack or bypass it, use SO_REUSEPORT listeners per event-loop. Target about 30 KB/conn so 1M is about 30 GB. Realistically choose 300k to 500k per node with 3x headroom, since a single failure would trigger a 1M reconnect storm.
  7. Prevention: Load test with realistic idle/active mix, alert on memory per connection and accept queue, jittered client reconnect.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not push to 1M just because it is possible; blast radius, GC pause size and failover capacity usually argue for more, smaller nodes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Do clients hit a port limit? -> A client connecting to one server IP:port is limited to about 28k to 64k ephemeral ports per local IP; add IPs or port ranges in the load generator.
  • Should it be epoll or io_uring? -> epoll is fine; the bottleneck is memory, not syscalls.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gateway sized for 1M connections per node died once, and the 1M simultaneous reconnects with TLS handshakes took the whole cluster down for 20 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes the 65k port myth; no memory model.
  • Hire: per-connection memory math, fd limits, event loop design.
  • Strong hire: also conntrack, TLS memory, reconnect storm blast radius, and a pragmatic per-node target.
